JEE-MATH-U01-001 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Sets and their representation · Easy · Class XI
The number of elements in the set P={x∈Z:x2−3x−10<0} is
  1. (A)4
  2. (B)7
  3. (C)6
  4. (D)8
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 6

x2−3x−10=(x−5)(x+2)<0 gives −2<x<5. The integers in this open interval are −1,0,1,2,3,4, so P has 6 elements.

Targets: Including the endpoints of a strict inequality.
Difficulty: One quadratic inequality, then counting integers.
Family: U01-A-setbuilder-count · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

Numerical-answer form: The number of elements in the set P={x∈Z:x2−3x−10<0} is Answer: 6
JEE-MATH-U01-002 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Sets and their representation · Easy · Class XI
In roster form, the set {x∈Z:x−112​∈N} (where N={1,2,3,…}) is
  1. (A){0,−1,−2,−3,−5,−11}
  2. (B){2,3,4,7,13}
  3. (C){1,2,3,4,6,12}
  4. (D){2,3,4,5,7,13}
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) {2,3,4,5,7,13}

x−112​ is a natural number exactly when x−1 is a positive divisor of 12, that is x−1∈{1,2,3,4,6,12}. Hence x∈{2,3,4,5,7,13}.

Targets: Confusing the values of x−1 with the values of x.
Difficulty: One divisibility condition, then a shift to list the elements.
Family: U01-A-setbuilder-divisor · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-003 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Power set · Easy · Class XI
If P(X) denotes the power set of a set X, then the number of elements in P(P(P(∅))) is
  1. (A)4
  2. (B)16
  3. (C)2
  4. (D)8
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 4

P(∅)={∅} has 1 element, so P(P(∅)) has 21=2 elements and P(P(P(∅))) has 22=4 elements.

Targets: Believing that P(∅) is empty or has two elements.
Difficulty: Apply n(P(X))=2n(X) three times.

JEE-MATH-U01-004 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Subsets · Easy · Class XI
The number of subsets of {1,2,3,4,5,6} that contain both 1 and 2 but do not contain 3 is
  1. (A)8
  2. (B)16
  3. (C)7
  4. (D)4
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 8

The elements 1 and 2 must be present and 3 must be absent. Each of the remaining elements 4,5,6 may or may not be included, giving 23=8 subsets.

Targets: Letting a forbidden element vary freely.
Difficulty: One multiplication-principle step.

JEE-MATH-U01-005 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Subsets · Easy · Class XI
A set X has 7 elements. The number of non-empty proper subsets of X is
  1. (A)127
  2. (B)64
  3. (C)126
  4. (D)128
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 126

X has 27=128 subsets. Excluding the empty set and X itself leaves 128−2=126 non-empty proper subsets.

Targets: Excluding only one of the empty set and the set itself.
Difficulty: Direct count with two exclusions.

JEE-MATH-U01-006 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Venn diagrams and cardinality · Easy · Class XI
In a group of 50 students, every student plays at least one of chess and carrom. If 40 students play chess and 26 play carrom, the number of students who play chess but not carrom is
  1. (A)10
  2. (B)24
  3. (C)14
  4. (D)16
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 24

Since every student plays at least one game, n(chess∪carrom)=50, so n(both)=40+26−50=16. Hence chess but not carrom is 40−16=24.

Targets: Confusing the intersection with the 'only' region.
Difficulty: Inclusion and exclusion once, then one subtraction.

JEE-MATH-U01-007 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Operations on sets · Easy · Class XI
Let U={1,2,3,…,10} be the universal set, P={x∈U:x is even} and Q={x∈U:x is prime}. Then (P∪Q)′ is
  1. (A){1,9}
  2. (B){1,3,5,7,9}
  3. (C){1}
  4. (D){9}
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) {1,9}

P={2,4,6,8,10} and Q={2,3,5,7}, so P∪Q={2,3,4,5,6,7,8,10} and (P∪Q)′={1,9}.

Targets: Misclassifying 1 or 9 as prime.
Difficulty: Two small sets, one union and one complement.

JEE-MATH-U01-008 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Operations on sets · Easy · Class XI
Let P={x∈Z:x2≤9} and Q={x∈Z:0≤x≤5}. Then (P−Q)∪(Q−P) is
  1. (A){−3,−2,−1,4,5}
  2. (B){−3,−2,−1}
  3. (C){−3,−2,−1,0,4,5}
  4. (D){0,1,2,3}
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) {−3,−2,−1,4,5}

P={−3,−2,−1,0,1,2,3} and Q={0,1,2,3,4,5}. Then P−Q={−3,−2,−1} and Q−P={4,5}, so the union is {−3,−2,−1,4,5}.

Targets: Computing only one of the two differences.
Difficulty: List two sets and take two differences.

JEE-MATH-U01-009 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Sets and their representation · Easy · Class XI
Which of the following sets is the empty set?
  1. (A){x∈Z:x2<2}
  2. (B){x∈Z:2<x2<5}
  3. (C){x∈R:x3+4x=0}
  4. (D){x∈R:x2+2x+3=0}
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) {x∈R:x2+2x+3=0}

For x2+2x+3=0 the discriminant is 4−12=−8<0, so there is no real root and the set is empty. The other sets are {0}, {−2,2} and {−1,0,1}, all non-empty.

Targets: Cancelling a variable factor and losing the zero solution.
Difficulty: Check four small sets; one discriminant.
Family: U01-A-empty-set · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-010 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Operations on sets · Easy · Class XI
If P and Q are sets such that P∪Q=P∩Q, then which of the following must be true?
  1. (A)P∩Q=∅
  2. (B)P⊊Q
  3. (C)P=Q
  4. (D)Q=∅
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) P=Q

Always P∩Q⊆P⊆P∪Q. If P∪Q=P∩Q, the chain forces P=P∩Q, and similarly Q=P∩Q. Hence P=Q; conversely P=Q makes the condition hold, so nothing more is forced.

Targets: Generalising from the special case of empty sets.
Difficulty: One sandwich argument with the basic inclusions.
Family: U01-A-union-equals-intersection · Check: BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-011 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Algebra of sets · Easy · Class XI
For any two subsets P and Q of a universal set U, the set (P∪Q)∩(P∪Q′) equals
  1. (A)P
  2. (B)U
  3. (C)∅
  4. (D)P∪Q
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) P

By the distributive law, (P∪Q)∩(P∪Q′)=P∪(Q∩Q′)=P∪∅=P.

Targets: Misapplying the distributive law of union over intersection.
Difficulty: One distributive step and one complement law.
Family: U01-A-law-distributive · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-012 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Venn diagrams and cardinality · Easy · Class XI
In a town of 10000 people, 65% read newspaper X, 40% read newspaper Y and 20% read both. The number of people who read neither newspaper is
  1. (A)1500
  2. (B)6000
  3. (C)3500
  4. (D)4500
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 1500

The percentage reading at least one is 65+40−20=85, so 15% read neither, that is 10015​×10000=1500 people.

Difficulty: One application of n(X∪Y) and a complement.

JEE-MATH-U01-013 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Power set · Easy · Class XI
If P={x∈Z:∣x−2∣<3}, then the number of elements in the power set of P is
  1. (A)128
  2. (B)64
  3. (C)32
  4. (D)25
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 32

∣x−2∣<3 gives −1<x<5, so P={0,1,2,3,4} with 5 elements. Its power set has 25=32 elements.

JEE-MATH-U01-014 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Sets and their representation · Easy · Class XI
Let P={1,{2},{1,2}}. Which of the following is true?
  1. (A)2∈P
  2. (B){2}∈P
  3. (C){2}⊆P
  4. (D){1,2}⊆P
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) {2}∈P

The elements of P are 1, {2} and {1,2}. So {2}∈P is true. Since 2 itself is not an element of P, both {2}⊆P and {1,2}⊆P fail, and 2∈P is false.

Targets: Confusing ∈ with ⊆ for sets whose elements are sets.
Difficulty: One careful reading of the roster.

JEE-MATH-U01-015 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Venn diagrams and cardinality · Medium · Class XI
In a survey of 100 students, 45 study Mathematics, 40 study Physics and 35 study Chemistry; 15 study Mathematics and Physics, 12 study Physics and Chemistry, 10 study Mathematics and Chemistry, and 5 study all three. The number of students who study none of the three subjects is
  1. (A)7
  2. (B)17
  3. (C)12
  4. (D)22
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 12

n(at least one)=45+40+35−15−12−10+5=88. Hence 100−88=12 students study none of the subjects.

JEE-MATH-U01-016 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Venn diagrams and cardinality · Medium · Class XI
In a housing society, 50 families read newspaper X, 40 read Y and 30 read Z. Also 20 read X and Y, 15 read Y and Z, 12 read X and Z, and 8 read all three. The number of families that read exactly one of the three newspapers is
  1. (A)26
  2. (B)34
  3. (C)50
  4. (D)81
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 50

Only X: 50−20−12+8=26; only Y: 40−20−15+8=13; only Z: 30−15−12+8=11. Exactly one is 26+13+11=50. Equivalently ∑n−2∑n(pairs)+3n(all)=120−94+24=50.

Targets: Subtracting the pairwise overlaps without adding back the triple region.
Difficulty: Region-by-region Venn counting with three sets.
Family: U01-A-venn3-exactly-one · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-017 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Venn diagrams and cardinality · Medium · Class XI
In a class of 60 students, 42 like tea and 35 like coffee. If M and m are the greatest and least possible numbers of students who like both drinks, then M−m equals
  1. (A)25
  2. (B)7
  3. (C)18
  4. (D)35
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 18

Let k like both. Then k≤min(42,35)=35, and n(tea∪coffee)=77−k≤60 gives k≥17. Both bounds are attained, so M=35, m=17 and M−m=18.

Targets: Forgetting that the union cannot exceed the class size.
Difficulty: Two bounds from two different constraints.

JEE-MATH-U01-018 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Algebra of sets · Medium · Class XI
Let P, Q, R be any three sets. Statement I: P−(Q∪R)=(P−Q)∩(P−R). Statement II: P−(Q∩R)=(P−Q)∩(P−R). In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  2. (B)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  3. (C)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  4. (D)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

x∈P−(Q∪R) means x∈P, x∈/Q and x∈/R, which is exactly x∈(P−Q)∩(P−R); so Statement I is true. By De Morgan, P−(Q∩R)=(P−Q)∪(P−R). For P={1,2}, Q={1}, R={2} we get P−(Q∩R)={1,2} but (P−Q)∩(P−R)=∅, so Statement II is false.

Targets: Not switching intersection and union when applying De Morgan's law.
Difficulty: One proof and one counterexample.
Family: U01-A-stmt-difference-demorgan · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-019 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Subsets · Medium · Class XI
The number of subsets of {1,2,3,…,10} that contain at least one odd number is
  1. (A)31
  2. (B)1023
  3. (C)512
  4. (D)992
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 992

Subsets with no odd number are the subsets of {2,4,6,8,10}, and there are 25=32 of them. Hence 210−25=1024−32=992 subsets contain at least one odd number.

Targets: Ignoring the free choice of the other elements, or counting non-empty subsets.
Difficulty: Complementary counting on subsets.

JEE-MATH-U01-020 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Power set · Medium · Class XI
For a set X, let P(X) denote its power set. Let X and Y be any two sets. Statement I: P(X)∪P(Y)=P(X∪Y). Statement II: P(X)∩P(Y)=P(X∩Y). In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  2. (B)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

S∈P(X)∩P(Y) means S⊆X and S⊆Y, that is S⊆X∩Y; so Statement II is true. For X={1}, Y={2}, the set {1,2} lies in P(X∪Y) but in neither P(X) nor P(Y), so Statement I is false.

Targets: Believing P distributes over union.
Difficulty: A proof and a counterexample with power sets.
Family: U01-A-stmt-power-set-ops · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-021 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Power set · Medium · Class XI
Let X and Y be finite sets with n(X)=5 and n(Y)=4. If the power set of X∩Y has 4 elements, then the number of elements in the power set of X∪Y is
  1. (A)128
  2. (B)512
  3. (C)32
  4. (D)44
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 128

2n(X∩Y)=4 gives n(X∩Y)=2. Then n(X∪Y)=5+4−2=7 and its power set has 27=128 elements.

JEE-MATH-U01-022 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Operations on sets · Medium · Class XI
Let P={x∈R:x2−5∣x∣+6=0} and Q={x∈R:x2−x−6≤0}. Then P∩Q is
  1. (A){−2,2,3}
  2. (B){2,3}
  3. (C){−3,−2,2,3}
  4. (D){−2,3}
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) {−2,2,3}

∣x∣2−5∣x∣+6=0 gives ∣x∣=2 or 3, so P={−3,−2,2,3}. Also (x−3)(x+2)≤0 gives Q=[−2,3]. Hence P∩Q={−2,2,3}.

JEE-MATH-U01-023 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Operations on sets · Medium · Class XI
Let P=[−2,3) and Q=(1,5] be subsets of R. Then P−Q is
  1. (A)[3,5]
  2. (B)(1,3)
  3. (C)[−2,1]
  4. (D)[−2,1)
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) [−2,1]

P−Q consists of points of [−2,3) not in (1,5]. Points of P greater than 1 lie in Q, while 1 itself does not lie in Q. Hence P−Q=[−2,1].

JEE-MATH-U01-024 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Algebra of sets · Medium · Class XI
For subsets P and Q of a universal set U, the set (P∩Q′)∪(P′∩Q′)∪(P∩Q) equals
  1. (A)Q′
  2. (B)U
  3. (C)P∩Q′
  4. (D)P∪Q′
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) P∪Q′

(P∩Q′)∪(P′∩Q′)=(P∪P′)∩Q′=Q′. Then Q′∪(P∩Q)=(Q′∪P)∩(Q′∪Q)=P∪Q′. In Venn terms, every region except Q−P is included, and (Q−P)′=P∪Q′.

JEE-MATH-U01-025 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Venn diagrams and cardinality · Medium · Class XI
For finite sets P and Q, n(P)=2n(Q), n(P∩Q)=10 and n(P∪Q)=50. Then n(P−Q) equals
  1. (A)10
  2. (B)40
  3. (C)20
  4. (D)30
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 30

Let n(Q)=k, so n(P)=2k. Then 50=2k+k−10 gives k=20 and n(P)=40. Hence n(P−Q)=40−10=30.

JEE-MATH-U01-026 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Venn diagrams and cardinality · Medium · Class XI
P and Q are finite sets with n(P)=10 and n(Q)=15. The number of different possible values of n(P∪Q) is
  1. (A)25
  2. (B)16
  3. (C)11
  4. (D)10
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 11

n(P∪Q)=25−n(P∩Q) and 0≤n(P∩Q)≤10, with every value possible. So n(P∪Q) takes the values 15,16,…,25, which are 11 values.

JEE-MATH-U01-027 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Subsets · Medium · Class XI
The number of ordered pairs (P,Q) of subsets of {1,2,3,4} such that P⊆Q is
  1. (A)65
  2. (B)256
  3. (C)81
  4. (D)16
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 81

For each element there are exactly three admissible options: in neither set, in Q only, or in both. Since P⊆Q forbids being in P only, the count is 34=81.

JEE-MATH-U01-028 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Algebra of sets · Medium · Class XI
Let P, Q, R be subsets of a universal set U. Statement I: If P∩Q=P∩R and P∪Q=P∪R, then Q=R. Statement II: P⊆Q if and only if P∩Q′=∅. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  2. (B)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  3. (C)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

For Statement I, Q=Q∩(P∪Q)=Q∩(P∪R)=(Q∩P)∪(Q∩R)=(P∩R)∪(Q∩R)=R∩(P∪Q)=R∩(P∪R)=R; so it is true. For Statement II, P∩Q′=∅ says no element of P lies outside Q, which is exactly P⊆Q; so it is true.

  1. (A)20
  2. (B)5
  3. (C)10
  4. (D)15
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 15

n(P)=35 and n(Q)=30. By De Morgan, P′∩Q′=(P∪Q)′, so n(P∪Q)=60−10=50. Hence n(P∩Q)=35+30−50=15.

Answer: (A) 8

2 must lie in both sets and 5 in neither. Each of 1,3,4 lies in the union but not the intersection, so it is in exactly one of P, Q: 2 choices each. The count is 23=8.

n(P∪Q)=20+25−8=37 and n((P∪Q)∩R)=n(P∩R)+n(Q∩R)−n(P∩Q∩R)=7+10−4=13. Hence n((P∪Q)∩R′)=37−13=24.

  1. (A)219

  3. (C)182

Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 210

(2n​)=28 gives n(n−1)=56, so n=8 and X has 28=256 subsets. Taking complements pairs each k-element subset with an (8−k)-element subset, so there are 8 subsets with seven elements and 1 with eight. Excluding sizes 0,1,2 (1+8+28=37) and sizes 7,8 (8+1=9) leaves 256−37−9=210.

In a group of 100 people, 70 like tea, 75 like coffee and 80 like juice. The least possible number of people who like all three drinks is
  1. (A)55
  2. (B)0
  3. (C)45
  4. (D)25
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 25

Each person who does not like all three misses at least one drink. The total number of misses is 30+25+20=75, so at most 75 people miss something and at least 100−75=25 like all three. This is attained when the 30, 25 and 20 non-likers are disjoint groups, so the least value is 25.

The number of non-empty subsets of {1,2,3,…,12} the product of whose elements is divisible by 6 is
  1. (A)3791
  2. (B)3792
  3. (C)3776
  4. (D)3072
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 3792

Count all subsets, including the empty one, whose product is not divisible by 6: either no element is even (26=64 subsets of {1,3,5,7,9,11}) or no element is a multiple of 3 (28=256 subsets of the other eight numbers), and both happen for the 24=16 subsets of {1,5,7,11}. So 64+256−16=304 subsets fail, the empty set among them. Hence 212−304=3792 non-empty subsets have product divisible by 6.

The number studying all three is 200−120−60=20. In n(X)+n(Y)+n(Z) a student is counted once for each language studied, so the sum is 120×1+60×2+20×3=300.

Answer: (C) 17

Let e1​, e3​ be the numbers liking exactly one and all three. Then e1​+20+e3​=100 and e1​+2(20)+3e3​=60+50+44=154. Subtracting, 20+2e3​=54, so e3​=17.

  1. (A)31
  2. (B)10
  3. (C)26
  4. (D)11
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 11

Let k play both. Then the number playing neither is 80−(95−k)=k−15. The conditions 0≤k−15≤10 give 15≤k≤25, and k≤45 is automatic. So k has 11 possible values.

  2. (B)4
  3. (C)32

Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 40

If k people like both, exactly one is (28−k)+(32−k)=60−2k. This is largest when k is smallest. Since 60−k≤50, k≥10, and k=10 is possible. So the greatest value is 60−20=40.

For subsets P, Q, R of a universal set U, the set (P−Q)∪(Q−R)∪(R−P) equals
  1. (A)P∪Q∪R
  2. (B)(P∪Q∪R)−(P∩Q∩R)
  3. (C)(P∩Q∩R)′
  4. (D)(P∪Q∪R)−[(P∩Q)∪(Q∩R)∪(R∩P)]
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) (P∪Q∪R)−(P∩Q∩R)

An element in none of the sets lies in no difference. An element in all three lies in no difference. If x lies in some but not all of the sets, then going round P→Q→R→P there is a step from a set containing x to one not containing it, so x lies in the corresponding difference. Hence the set is (P∪Q∪R)−(P∩Q∩R).

With e1​,e2​,e3​ the numbers joining exactly one, two, three activities, e1​+e2​+e3​=100 and e1​+2e2​+3e3​=60+50+45=155, so e2​+2e3​=55 and e3​≤27. n(X×Y)=6, so there are 26=64 relations. Those with fewer than two pairs are the empty relation and the 6 singletons. Hence 64−1−6=57.

x=15−2y≥1 gives y=1,2,…,7, so R={(13,1),(11,2),…,(1,7)}. The domain of R−1 equals the range of R, which is {1,2,…,7}.

Answer: (D) 79

For the domain to be X, each of the 4 elements must be related to a non-empty subset of Y: 3 choices each, 34=81 relations. Among these, the range is only {p} in one case (every element related to p alone) and only {q} in one case. So the count is 81−2=79.

Answer: (B) reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive

All of (1,1),(2,2),(3,3) are present, so R is reflexive. (1,2)∈R but (2,1)∈/R, so it is not symmetric. (1,2),(2,3)∈R but (1,3)∈/R, so it is not transitive.

Answer: (D) reflexive and transitive but not symmetric

Every (a,a) is present, so R is reflexive. (1,2)∈R but (2,1)∈/R, so it is not symmetric. The only chains through distinct elements are (1,3),(3,2), needing (1,2)∈R, which holds; chains using a diagonal pair are automatic. So R is transitive.

A reflexive relation must contain all 4 pairs (a,a). Each of the remaining 16−4=12 ordered pairs may be included or not, giving 212 reflexive relations.

JEE-MATH-U01-066 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Types of relations · Easy · Class XII
Let X be a non-empty set. Statement I: The identity relation IX​={(a,a):a∈X} is an equivalence relation on X. Statement II: The empty relation on X is symmetric and transitive. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  2. (B)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

IX​ contains every (a,a), so it is reflexive; (a,b)∈IX​ means a=b, so symmetry and transitivity hold. The empty relation has no pair (a,b), so the conditions 'if (a,b)∈R then ...' are vacuously true; it is symmetric and transitive (though not reflexive on a non-empty set). Both statements are true.

Let L be the set of all lines in a plane, and let R={(ℓ1​,ℓ2​):ℓ1​⊥ℓ2​} on L. Then R is

  3. (C)reflexive, symmetric and transitive
  4. (D)reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive

No line is perpendicular to itself, so R is not reflexive. If ℓ1​⊥ℓ2​ then ℓ2​⊥ℓ1​, so R is symmetric. If ℓ1​⊥ℓ2​ and ℓ2​⊥ℓ3​, then ℓ1​∥ℓ3​, not perpendicular, so R is not transitive.

On R, define aRb if and only if ∣a−b∣≤1. Then R is
  1. (A)reflexive and symmetric but not transitive

Answer: (A) reflexive and symmetric but not transitive

∣a−a∣=0≤1, so R is reflexive. ∣a−b∣=∣b−a∣, so it is symmetric. But 0R1 and 1R2 while ∣0−2∣=2>1, so it is not transitive.

Answer: (C) 4

Reflexivity needs (1,1),(2,2),(3,3). Transitivity with (1,2),(2,3) needs (1,3). The relation {(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(1,2),(2,3),(1,3)} is reflexive and transitive, so the minimum number added is 4.

Reflexivity fixes all 4 diagonal pairs. Symmetry ties (a,b) to (b,a), so each of the (24​)=6 unordered pairs {a,b} is either fully in or fully out. Hence the count is 26=64.

The pairs force 1,2,3 into one class, and 4 may stay alone. The smallest such relation has classes {1,2,3} and {4}, so it has 32+12=10 ordered pairs.

  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Intersection: every (a,a) lies in both, symmetry passes to the intersection, and if (a,b),(b,c) lie in both, then (a,c) lies in both; so Statement II is true. Union: on {1,2,3} take R1​ with classes {1,2},{3} and R2​ with classes {2,3},{1}. Then (1,2),(2,3)∈R1​∪R2​ but (1,3)∈/R1​∪R2​, so Statement I is false.

Targets: Assuming transitivity survives unions.
Difficulty: A general proof and a counterexample.

JEE-MATH-U01-084 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Types of relations · Medium · Class XII
On Z, define aRb if and only if a2−7ab+6b2=0. Then R is
  1. (A)reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
  2. (B)reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
  3. (C)reflexive and symmetric but not transitive
  4. (D)reflexive, symmetric and transitive
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive

a2−7ab+6b2=(a−b)(a−6b), so aRb means a=b or a=6b. Reflexive: a=a. Not symmetric: 6=6⋅1 but 1=6 and 1=36. Not transitive: 36R6 and 6R1, but 36=1 and 36=6.

JEE-MATH-U01-085 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Equivalence relations · Difficult · Class XII
On X={1,2,3,…,12}, let R={(a,b):3 divides a−b} and S={(a,b):4 divides a−b}. The number of ordered pairs in R∪S is
  1. (A)72
  2. (B)62
  3. (C)60
  4. (D)84
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 72

R has classes of sizes 4,4,4 (residues modulo 3), so n(R)=48. S has classes of sizes 3,3,3,3, so n(S)=36. (a,b)∈R∩S means 12∣(a−b), which in X forces a=b, so n(R∩S)=12. Hence n(R∪S)=48+36−12=72.

JEE-MATH-U01-086 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Counting relations with properties · Difficult · Class XII
The number of relations on {1,2,3} that are symmetric and transitive but not reflexive is
  1. (A)5
  2. (B)15
  3. (C)9
  4. (D)10
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 10

A symmetric transitive relation is an equivalence relation on the subset Y of elements a with (a,a)∈R, since (a,b)∈R forces (a,a),(b,b)∈R. So the count is ∑k​(k3​)Bk​=1+3⋅1+3⋅2+1⋅5=15, where Bk​ is the number of partitions of a k-set. Those with Y the whole set are the 5 equivalence relations, so 15−5=10 are not reflexive.

Difficulty: Requires the structure of symmetric transitive relations and a careful sum over subsets.

JEE-MATH-U01-087 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Counting relations with properties · Difficult · Class XII
The number of relations on {1,2,3} that are both reflexive and transitive is
  1. (A)64
  2. (B)29
  3. (C)5
  4. (D)19
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 29

Group by the classes of mutually related elements. All three distinct and no two-way pairs: the off-diagonal part must be a transitive 'one-way' pattern, giving 19: the identity (1), one extra pair (6), two extra pairs with a common smallest or common largest element (6), and a full chain such as (1,2),(2,3),(1,3) (6). With exactly one two-way pair, say {1,2}, the block {1,2} relates to 3 in one of 3 ways (no link, block to 3, 3 to block), giving 3×3=9. With all three mutually related: 1. Total 19+9+1=29.

Targets: Ignoring two-way pairs or adding symmetry that is not required.
Difficulty: Casework over the block structure; easy to miss a family of cases.
Family: U01-B-count-ref-tr · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U01-088 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Counting relations with properties · Difficult · Class XII
The number of relations on {1,2,3} that contain (1,2) and (2,3) and are reflexive and transitive but not symmetric is
  1. (A)4
  2. (B)8
  3. (C)3
  4. (D)5
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 3

Such an R contains the diagonal, (1,2),(2,3) and, by transitivity, (1,3). The only other possible pairs are (2,1),(3,2),(3,1). Adding (3,1) forces (3,2) via (3,1),(1,2) and (2,1) via (2,3),(3,1), giving the universal (symmetric) relation. Adding (2,1) and (3,2) together forces (3,1). So the valid choices are: nothing, (2,1) alone, or (3,2) alone, each of which is transitive and not symmetric. The count is 3.

Targets: Not following forced pairs through transitivity.
Difficulty: Casework where each addition forces others through transitivity.

Answer: (B) 37

There are B5​=52 equivalence relations on a five-element set. Those with 1,2 in the same class correspond to partitions of the four objects {12},3,4,5, so there are B4​=15 of them. Hence 52−15=37.

JEE-MATH-U01-092 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Equivalence relations · Difficult · Class XII
Statement I: The relation R on Z given by aRb if and only if a+2b is divisible by 3 is not an equivalence relation. Statement II: The relation T on Z given by aTb if and only if a+3b is divisible by 5 is an equivalence relation. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  2. (B)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  4. (D)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Since a+2b=(a−b)+3b, 3∣(a+2b) if and only if 3∣(a−b), which is congruence modulo 3, an equivalence relation; so Statement I is false. For T, aTa needs 5∣4a, which fails for a=1; so T is not reflexive and Statement II is false.

JEE-MATH-U01-093 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Types of relations · Difficult · Class XII
Let X={1,2,3,4,5}. The number of ordered pairs in the smallest transitive relation on X that contains (1,2),(2,3),(3,4),(4,5) and (5,1) is
  1. (A)25
  2. (B)15
  3. (C)10
  4. (D)20
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 25

Following the cycle, every element reaches every other element, so (a,b) must be in the relation for all a=b. Then (a,b),(b,a) force (a,a). So the smallest transitive relation is all of X×X, with 25 ordered pairs.

  1. (A)96
  2. (B)110
  3. (C)26
  4. (D)116
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 116

A symmetric relation consists of d diagonal pairs and u unordered off-diagonal pairs, each contributing 2 ordered pairs, so d+2u=6 with d≤4, u≤6. Cases: d=0,u=3: (36​)=20; d=2,u=2: (24​)(26​)=90; d=4,u=1: (16​)=6. Total 20+90+6=116.

Answer: (B) 216

A function from a 3-element set has at most 3 distinct images, so it can never cover all 6 elements of Q. Hence no function from P to Q is onto, and all 63=216 functions are not onto.

  4. (D)f(x)=x3−3x2+3x
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) f(x)=x3−3x2+3x

x3−3x2+3x=(x−1)3+1. If (a−1)3+1=(b−1)3+1 then (a−1)3=(b−1)3, so a=b; hence it is one-one. Each of the other three takes the value 0 at two different points: x3−x2 at 0,1; x2+2x at 0,−2; x3−4x at 0,±2.

  2. (B)one-one but not onto
  3. (C)onto but not one-one
  4. (D)bijective
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) one-one but not onto

If 2a+3=2b+3 then a=b, so f is one-one. But f(n)≥5 and is always odd, so for example 1 (or 6) has no pre-image in N; thus f is not onto.

  2. (B)36
  3. (C)72
  4. (D)81
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 36

Total functions =34=81. Functions missing a given element: 24=16, three choices; missing two given elements: 1, three choices. By inclusion-exclusion, onto functions =81−3⋅16+3⋅1=36. Equivalently, choose the pair sharing an image, 4C2​=6, then assign three blocks to three letters, 3!=6: 36.

f(x)=x2 for x≥0 and f(x)=−x2 for x<0. On [0,∞) it increases and takes all values in [0,∞); on (−∞,0) it increases and takes all values in (−∞,0). These ranges are disjoint and together give R, so f is one-one and onto, i.e. bijective.

Answer and solution

Answer: (D) onto but not one-one

f(0)=0 and f(3​)=33​−33​=0, so f is not one-one. For any real c, the cubic equation x3−3x−c=0 has real coefficients, so its non-real roots occur in conjugate pairs; with three roots in all, at least one root is real. That real root is a pre-image of c, so f is onto.

Let N={1,2,3,…} and let f:N→N be defined by f(n)=n+1 if n is odd and f(n)=n−1 if n is even. Then f is

  2. (B)onto but not one-one
  3. (C)bijective
  4. (D)one-one but not onto
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) bijective

f swaps 1↔2, 3↔4, and so on. Odd inputs go to even outputs and even inputs to odd outputs, each branch is one-one, so f is one-one. Every even m equals f(m−1) and every odd m equals f(m+1), so f is onto. Indeed f(f(n))=n. Hence f is bijective.

JEE-MATH-U01-134 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Functions · Difficult · Class XII
Let P={1,2,3,4}. Statement I: The number of functions f:P→P with f(f(x))=f(x) for every x∈P is 41. Statement II: The number of functions f:P→P for which f∘f is a constant function is 92. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.

  2. (B)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  3. (C)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Statement I: f(f(x))=f(x) means f fixes every element of its range. For a range of k elements, choose it in 4Ck​ ways and send each of the other 4−k elements into it in k4−k ways: 4⋅1+6⋅4+4⋅3+1⋅1=41, so Statement I is true. Statement II: if f(f(x))=c for all x, then f(c)=f(f(f(c)))=c. Let S be the set of elements other than c with f(x)=c; every other element x=c has f(x)=c and f(f(x))=c, so f(x)∈S, and conversely every such map works. With s=∣S∣ out of the 3 elements other than c, the count is 3Cs​s3−s, i.e. 0+3+6+1=10 for each c, so 4⋅10=40=92. Statement II is false.

JEE-MATH-U01-135 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Functions · Difficult · Class XII
For an integer k, let fk​:R→R be defined by fk​(x)=kx+3∣x∣. The number of integers k with −10≤k≤10 for which fk​ is bijective is
  1. (A)14
  2. (B)8
  3. (C)7
  4. (D)16
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 14

For x≥0, fk​(x)=(k+3)x; for x<0, fk​(x)=(k−3)x. If the two slopes have the same sign (both non-zero), fk​ is strictly monotonic with range R, hence bijective. If they have opposite signs or one is zero, fk​ is not one-one (and its range is a half-line). So we need (k+3)(k−3)>0, i.e. ∣k∣>3: k=4,…,10 and k=−10,…,−4, which is 7+7=14 values.

JEE-MATH-U01-136 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Functions · Difficult · Class XII
The function f:R→R, f(x)=2ex−e−x​, is a bijection. Then f−1(x) equals
  1. (A)loge​(x2+1​−x)
  2. (B)loge​(x+x2+1​)
  3. (C)loge​(x+x2−1​)
  4. (D)loge​(2x+x2+4​​)
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) loge​(x+x2+1​)

Let y=2ex−e−x​ and u=ex>0. Then u2−2yu−1=0, so u=y±y2+1​. Since y2+1​>∣y∣, only u=y+y2+1​ is positive. Hence x=loge​(y+y2+1​) and f−1(x)=loge​(x+x2+1​).

Targets: Mishandling the quadratic in ex or the choice of the positive root.
Difficulty: Substitution to a quadratic, solving, and rejecting a root.

JEE-MATH-U01-137 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Functions · Difficult · Class XII
Let f:R→S be defined by f(x)=x2+x+1x2−x+1​. If f is onto, then S equals
  1. (A)[1,3]
  2. (B)[31​,3]
  3. (C)[31​,1]
  4. (D)(31​,3)
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) [31​,3]

Put y=f(x): (y−1)x2+(y+1)x+(y−1)=0. For y=1, a real x exists iff (y+1)2−4(y−1)2≥0, i.e. (3−y)(3y−1)≥0, so 31​≤y≤3; y=1 is attained at x=0. Also f(1)=31​ and f(−1)=3. So the range is [31​,3], and onto requires S to equal it.

JEE-MATH-U01-138 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Functions · Difficult · Class XII
Let f:R→R be defined by f(x)=x+2 for x<0 and f(x)=x2−1 for x≥0. The number of real solutions of (f∘f)(x)=0 is
  1. (A)3
  2. (B)2
  3. (C)5
  4. (D)4
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 3

First f(y)=0: for y<0, y=−2; for y≥0, y=1. Now f(x)=−2: x+2=−2 gives x=−4; x2−1=−2 has no solution. And f(x)=1: x+2=1 gives x=−1; x2−1=1 with x≥0 gives x=2​. So the solutions are −4,−1,2​: three in all.

JEE-MATH-U01-139 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Functions · Difficult · Class XII
The number of one-one functions f:{1,2,3}→{1,2,3,4,5} such that f(i)=i for i=1,2,3 is
  1. (A)60
  2. (B)32
  3. (C)34
  4. (D)24
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 32

Total one-one functions: 5P3​=60. With f(i)=i for a given i: 4P2​=12, three choices of i. For two given fixed points: 3P1​=3, three pairs. All three fixed: 1. By inclusion-exclusion, 60−36+9−1=32.

Targets: Treating the choices as independent of earlier choices.
Difficulty: Four-term inclusion-exclusion with permutations.

JEE-MATH-U01-140 · Unit 1: Sets, Relations and Functions · Functions · Difficult · Class XII
The number of functions f:{1,2,3,4}→{1,2,3,4,5,6} such that f(1)≤f(2)≤f(3)≤f(4) is
  1. (A)15
  2. (B)126
  3. (C)210
  4. (D)84
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 126

A non-decreasing f is determined by how many of the 4 inputs take each value 1,…,6, i.e. by non-negative integers n1​+⋯+n6​=4. The number of solutions is 4+6−1C4​=9C4​=126. Equivalently, g(i)=f(i)+i−1 is strictly increasing into {1,…,9}, giving 9C4​.

Targets: Treating non-decreasing as strictly increasing, or misapplying stars and bars.
Difficulty: Bijection to multisets or stars and bars; non-obvious route.
Family: U01-C-count-nondecreasing · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED
